What’s Still Needed to Verify Tucson’s 2025 Housing Results?

Sources checked November 9, 2026.

What the record shows. Tucson announced a public-comment draft of its Program Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER), covering July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026. The City’s reports index still lists the PY2024 CAPER as its latest entry.

What’s still open. We have yet to verify the final PY2025 report or its submission to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The records needed are the final report, its detailed spending and outcome tables, and dated records of submission and HUD receipt.

Read the source. Tucson’s August 31 draft notice · City reports index

County Allocations and PRICE

What we know: $8.7 million in FY2027 County allocations and $2,986,331 in County-approved PRICE scopes. A separate additional $1 million request was tabled indefinitely.

Still unanswered: Executed agreements, actual County spending and matched household outcomes. Federal reporting of $78,172.27 through August 2026 concerns the City’s entire PRICE award, not County spending.

Who pays to weatherize existing homes?

Research review: November 24, 2026.

Tucson Electric Power reported helping fund energy-efficiency retrofits in 65 homes in 2025. TEP identifies 60 in its Weatherized Home category, which combines utility and other funding, and five in Energy Ease Plus, which uses utility funding only. TEP says it counts a job as complete after all measures have been installed and inspected. TEP’s 2025 filing · Installation table.

TEP funds its energy-efficiency programs through a charge on customer bills. A 2025 Pima County agreement approved by the Board of Supervisors allowed TEP to reimburse up to $150,000 for qualifying weatherization work outside Tucson and South Tucson. This was a reimbursement limit. Separately, Pima County accepted $168,620 from the U.S. Department of Energy and $566,252 from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, through the Arizona Department of Housing, under its July 2024–June 2025 agreement. Those grants support energy upgrades and related health and safety repairs in existing homes. Utility charge · County utility agreement · Federal grant announcement.

The records reviewed do not show what TEP reimbursed for calendar year 2025, how many homes each partner finished, or which of the 65 homes used specific public grants. These figures describe upgrades to existing homes and do not measure new units or HUD spending.

County Housing Funding: What the Records Show

Published: November 8, 2026, 10:48 a.m. MST (Tucson). Research updated: November 8, 2026, 10:41:35 AM MST (Tucson). Source dates and financial reporting periods are identified below.

Pima County approved $8.7 million for housing and stability programs. A separate $1 million request was tabled indefinitely. The County also approved $2.99 million in PRICE agreement scopes for home repairs and eviction assistance. These approvals and targets do not establish actual County spending or households served.

County Housing Allocations

On September 8, 2026, the Board approved $5 million for gap funding and $3.7 million for housing stability, totaling $8.7 million for FY2027. The separate additional $1 million request was tabled indefinitely. These are allocation decisions, not evidence of payments or completed assistance. The posted meeting summary expressly is not approved minutes. Meeting summary, PDF p. 6 · Official allocation action

County PRICE Agreement Scopes

The two County-approved PRICE agreements total $2,986,331: $2,009,932 for home repairs and $976,399 for eviction-prevention and legal services. Their stated term is July 1, 2026–June 30, 2029. These are components of existing PRICE grant funding, not additional federal revenue to add to the full award. Repair agreement · Eviction-prevention agreement · Repair approval · Eviction-prevention approval

The records identify planned work and targets. They do not establish completed repairs, actual payments, legal outcomes or households already assisted. The posted execution pages contain blank mayor, Board chair and clerk signature lines; attorney review is present. Fully executed counterparts and later amendments remain unverified. Blank lines in a posted packet do not prove that no agreement was later executed.

Later expenditures and actual household outcomes remain unverified. The difference between the award and reported outlays is not a verified available balance, and these records alone do not establish improper withholding or misuse.

County One Stop Rapid-Rehousing Outcomes

The TPCH FY2026 scorecard reports 17 of 24 County One Stop rapid-rehousing leavers exiting to permanent housing (70.8%) for July 1, 2025–June 1, 2026, with no excluded leavers. A separate earlier group had 13 of 24 people return to homelessness within 12 months (54.2%); that cohort exited to permanent housing during June 1, 2024–June 1, 2025. These are people in one project and two different cohorts, not a Countywide success rate or one group’s retention result. Matched reporting periods, inclusion rules and aggregate follow-up outcomes are needed before comparing costs or broader program performance.

Original November 6 write-up

Published: November 6, 2026, 4:48 p.m. MST (Tucson). Source: November 5, 2026 County memo, pages 2–3.

What Did the County Report?

Pima County reported $2.49 million spent and 925 households served across six housing assistance strategies in the first quarter of FY27. The figures are subject to reconciliation; the report does not say whether households appear in more than one category.

What Doesn’t Add Up?

  • Rapid-Rehousing: The table lists 95 households, but the narrative totals 98.
  • Rapid-Rehousing Average: The reported costs divided by 95 equal $3,671.42, not the printed $3,290.42.
  • Home-Repair Average: The reported costs divided by 91 equal $2,279.52, not the printed $2,280.52.

What Funding Is Involved?

The $207,436 home-repair line is listed under County CDBG agencies. CDBG is a federal HUD program, but the memo doesn’t identify the specific award. It separately lists $111,045 as the County-funded portion of Affordable Housing Fund repair and weatherization work.

What’s Next?

A reconciled table and an explanation of the counts and calculations would clarify the results. The discrepancies alone do not establish misuse of funds.

Source: Pima County, One Pima Initiative: Fiscal Year 27 First Quarter Update, November 5, 2026, page 2; rapid-rehousing narrative, page 3.

Tucson’s CDBG Funding: What Adds Up, and What Still Needs Explaining

We withdrew the earlier $944,972.60 comparison because it combined regular CDBG and CDBG-CV, which are reported separately. The $1,284,589.71 difference within regular CDBG remains unexplained; it does not establish missing funds.

Summary revised: November 6, 2026, 9:52 a.m. MST (Tucson). Original correction history and source dates follow unchanged.

Posted: November 6, 2026, 7:42 a.m. MST (Tucson). Source dates are identified below.

What Did We Find, and Why Does It Matter?

The resource figures and ending balance in Tucson’s CDBG reports add up. The remaining question is more focused: how does the City’s spending narrative connect to the corrected financial report for its regular CDBG program? Federal guidance now helps separate that question from coronavirus-response funding. Financial summary · Spending narrative · OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61

For residents, the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) can mean home repairs, better public facilities and services for low-income people. Connecting the dollars to completed work helps show what that funding delivered. City’s description of CDBG-supported work

What Adds Up?

Program income, money generated by CDBG-funded activities, accounts for the previously questioned resource difference. The full financial report also includes money carried over from the previous year:

  • $5,068,664 annual grant + $349,468 program income = $5,418,132. The income is already included; adding it again would double-count it.
  • $3,778,221.56 opening balance + $5,418,132 grant and income = $9,196,353.56 in total resources.
  • $9,196,353.56 resources − $4,717,936.37 expenditures = $4,478,417.19 ending balance.

Those calculations reproduce the City’s resource total and ending balance. The reported balance does not establish money available for new work today. Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

Which Spending Figures Should We Compare?

The Office of Management and Budget’s 2025 Compliance Supplement says the standard PR26 CDBG Financial Summary Report has been restricted to annual formula grants since September 14, 2020. A separate PR26 report covers CDBG-CV, the CARES Act coronavirus-response grants. OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61

That makes the regular CDBG figures the appropriate starting point:

  • Corrected standard PR-26 expenditures: $4,717,936.37.
  • CDBG spending stated in the narrative: $3,433,346.66.
  • Difference requiring reconciliation: $1,284,589.71.

The summary table’s $4,717,936 agrees with the corrected PR-26 after rounding. The narrative says the final CDBG draw occurred after June 30, 2025, which may help explain the difference. But the records reviewed do not show which transactions connect the two figures or establish that timing explains the full amount. Summary table and narrative, PDF p. 13 · Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

Why Set Aside the Earlier $944,972.60 Comparison?

That calculation subtracted both the $3,433,346.66 CDBG narrative and the $339,616.74 CDBG-CV narrative from the rounded $4,717,936 summary total. It mixed the separately reported grant programs. HUD Oversight: What the Public Record Shows

What happens when someone reports housing discrimination? How does HUD check whether assisted housing meets federal standards? Audits and agency reports answer parts of those questions. They don’t tell us whether a particular complaint was handled correctly or whether a specific property is in compliance today.

Fair housing: from inquiry to investigation

  • When an inquiry is closed. Reporting possible discrimination starts an inquiry; it does not automatically open a formal investigation. A 2022 Inspector General audit found at least one documentation deficiency in 42 of 83 sampled inquiries closed at intake. Records did not always explain why an inquiry was closed, how jurisdiction was decided, or whether the person received proper notice. The Inspector General closed both recommendations in March 2024. That is not a new measurement of how well HUD handles inquiries. Audit · Recommendation status
  • Once a complaint is filed. A 2024 audit reported that 70.2% of HUD’s Title VIII investigations exceeded 100 days in its 2020–2022 analysis. The law allows longer when completing an investigation within 100 days is impracticable. In September 2026, HUD reported a 46% reduction in the backlog it inherited. A smaller backlog is a different measure from the share of investigations completed within 100 days. Audit · HUD update
  • Disability accommodations. GAO found that HUD did not systematically collect data on accommodation requests across its three largest rental assistance programs and lacked a comprehensive written oversight strategy. GAO lists both recommendations as open. This finding concerns federal oversight, not the handling of any individual request. GAO report and recommendation status

What HUD checks at assisted properties

  • Civil-rights monitoring. A 2025 Inspector General audit found that HUD and its contractors completed civil-rights monitoring in 12 of 132 sampled management and occupancy reviews. That measures whether the reviews included the required monitoring, not how many properties violated civil-rights laws. Audit
  • Physical inspections. In August 2026, the Inspector General reported that HUD had not inspected all covered properties under its newer standards. HUD generally could not determine the next inspection dates for properties associated with small and rural housing authorities, including some that had failed inspection. The audit does not establish conditions at any specific Arizona property. Audit

Access to public records

HUD’s Chief FOIA Officer reported 1,092 backlogged requests nationwide at the end of FY2025, citing staffing losses and more numerous and complex requests. The figure is not an Arizona count and doesn’t tell us how long any individual request took. HUD report, section V.C

Arizona example: a settlement, not a finding

In 2021, the Housing Authority of Maricopa County agreed to corrective steps, including staff training, after a tenant alleged that a designated contact did not receive a recertification notice. The agreement was not an admission or a HUD finding of discrimination. It does not establish the authority’s current practices. Signed agreement

What HAP will look for next

For Arizona, we’ll look for aggregate counts of inquiries received, closed at intake, referred, and accepted for investigation, along with processing times and types of outcomes. We’ll track accommodation requests made to housing providers separately. Those records could show where people encounter delays without exposing anyone’s case file.

More on staffing and sources

GAO interviewed 20 selected housing organizations about HUD’s workforce changes. Nearly all said experienced HUD contacts had left, making programs harder to navigate. Those are documented experiences from the organizations interviewed, not a nationwide or Arizona rate. GAO workforce report

Tucson’s CDBG Funding: What Adds Up, and What Still Needs Explaining

We withdrew the earlier $944,972.60 comparison because it combined regular CDBG and CDBG-CV, which are reported separately. The $1,284,589.71 difference within regular CDBG remains unexplained; it does not establish missing funds.

Summary revised: November 6, 2026, 9:52 a.m. MST (Tucson). Original correction history and source dates follow unchanged.

Posted: November 6, 2026, 7:42 a.m. MST (Tucson). Source dates are identified below.

What Did We Find, and Why Does It Matter?

The resource figures and ending balance in Tucson’s CDBG reports add up. The remaining question is more focused: how does the City’s spending narrative connect to the corrected financial report for its regular CDBG program? Federal guidance now helps separate that question from coronavirus-response funding. Financial summary · Spending narrative · OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61

For residents, the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) can mean home repairs, better public facilities and services for low-income people. Connecting the dollars to completed work helps show what that funding delivered. City’s description of CDBG-supported work

What Adds Up?

Program income, money generated by CDBG-funded activities, accounts for the previously questioned resource difference. The full financial report also includes money carried over from the previous year:

  • $5,068,664 annual grant + $349,468 program income = $5,418,132. The income is already included; adding it again would double-count it.
  • $3,778,221.56 opening balance + $5,418,132 grant and income = $9,196,353.56 in total resources.
  • $9,196,353.56 resources − $4,717,936.37 expenditures = $4,478,417.19 ending balance.

Those calculations reproduce the City’s resource total and ending balance. The reported balance does not establish money available for new work today. Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

Which Spending Figures Should We Compare?

The Office of Management and Budget’s 2025 Compliance Supplement says the standard PR26 CDBG Financial Summary Report has been restricted to annual formula grants since September 14, 2020. A separate PR26 report covers CDBG-CV, the CARES Act coronavirus-response grants. OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61

That makes the regular CDBG figures the appropriate starting point:

  • Corrected standard PR-26 expenditures: $4,717,936.37.
  • CDBG spending stated in the narrative: $3,433,346.66.
  • Difference requiring reconciliation: $1,284,589.71.

The summary table’s $4,717,936 agrees with the corrected PR-26 after rounding. The narrative says the final CDBG draw occurred after June 30, 2025, which may help explain the difference. But the records reviewed do not show which transactions connect the two figures or establish that timing explains the full amount. Summary table and narrative, PDF p. 13 · Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

Why Set Aside the Earlier $944,972.60 Comparison?

HUD Oversight: What the Public Record Shows

What happens when someone reports housing discrimination? How does HUD check whether assisted housing meets federal standards? Audits and agency reports answer parts of those questions. They don’t tell us whether a particular complaint was handled correctly or whether a specific property is in compliance today.

Fair housing: from inquiry to investigation

  • When an inquiry is closed. Reporting possible discrimination starts an inquiry; it does not automatically open a formal investigation. A 2022 Inspector General audit found at least one documentation deficiency in 42 of 83 sampled inquiries closed at intake. Records did not always explain why an inquiry was closed, how jurisdiction was decided, or whether the person received proper notice. The Inspector General closed both recommendations in March 2024. That is not a new measurement of how well HUD handles inquiries. Audit · Recommendation status
  • Once a complaint is filed. A 2024 audit reported that 70.2% of HUD’s Title VIII investigations exceeded 100 days in its 2020–2022 analysis. The law allows longer when completing an investigation within 100 days is impracticable. In September 2026, HUD reported a 46% reduction in the backlog it inherited. A smaller backlog is a different measure from the share of investigations completed within 100 days. Audit · HUD update
  • Disability accommodations. GAO found that HUD did not systematically collect data on accommodation requests across its three largest rental assistance programs and lacked a comprehensive written oversight strategy. GAO lists both recommendations as open. This finding concerns federal oversight, not the handling of any individual request. GAO report and recommendation status

What HUD checks at assisted properties

  • Civil-rights monitoring. A 2025 Inspector General audit found that HUD and its contractors completed civil-rights monitoring in 12 of 132 sampled management and occupancy reviews. That measures whether the reviews included the required monitoring, not how many properties violated civil-rights laws. Audit
  • Physical inspections. In August 2026, the Inspector General reported that HUD had not inspected all covered properties under its newer standards. HUD generally could not determine the next inspection dates for properties associated with small and rural housing authorities, including some that had failed inspection. The audit does not establish conditions at any specific Arizona property. Audit

Access to public records

HUD’s Chief FOIA Officer reported 1,092 backlogged requests nationwide at the end of FY2025, citing staffing losses and more numerous and complex requests. The figure is not an Arizona count and doesn’t tell us how long any individual request took. HUD report, section V.C

Arizona example: a settlement, not a finding

In 2021, the Housing Authority of Maricopa County agreed to corrective steps, including staff training, after a tenant alleged that a designated contact did not receive a recertification notice. The agreement was not an admission or a HUD finding of discrimination. It does not establish the authority’s current practices. Signed agreement

What HAP will look for next

For Arizona, we’ll look for aggregate counts of inquiries received, closed at intake, referred, and accepted for investigation, along with processing times and types of outcomes. We’ll track accommodation requests made to housing providers separately. Those records could show where people encounter delays without exposing anyone’s case file.

More on staffing and sources

GAO interviewed 20 selected housing organizations about HUD’s workforce changes. Nearly all said experienced HUD contacts had left, making programs harder to navigate. Those are documented experiences from the organizations interviewed, not a nationwide or Arizona rate. GAO workforce report
